chapter_summary:
Advanced debugging in Linux moves beyond simple log analysis and process monitoring to deep dives into application and kernel behavior. This level of troubleshooting is often required for intermittent issues, performance anomalies, or crashes that defy conventional diagnosis. The GNU Debugger (`GDB`) is a powerful tool for inspecting the internal state of a program, whether it's a running process or a core dump from a crashed application. `GDB` allows you to set breakpoints, step through code, inspect variables, and examine the call stack. For post-mortem analysis, you can load a core dump (`gdb <executable> <core_dump_file>`) to see the state of the program at the exact moment of the crash, including the stack trace and variable values, which is invaluable for identifying the root cause of segmentation faults or other fatal errors. For live debugging, `gdb attach <PID>` allows you to connect to a running process, though this should be done with extreme caution on production systems as it can pause the application. Common mistakes include not having debug symbols installed for the executable, which makes `GDB` output less informative.

For performance analysis, `perf` is an indispensable tool provided by the Linux kernel. `perf` collects and analyzes performance counter data, giving insights into CPU usage, cache misses, branch predictions, and system calls. `perf stat <command>` runs a command and provides a summary of performance events. `perf record -g <command>` records performance data, including call graphs, which can then be analyzed with `perf report`. This allows you to identify hot spots in code, functions that consume the most CPU cycles, or areas with high cache miss rates. For example, `perf record -g sleep 10` followed by `perf report` can show the kernel functions called during the sleep. `perf top` provides a `top`-like interface for real-time performance monitoring. `perf` is particularly useful for optimizing applications and identifying performance bottlenecks that aren't immediately obvious from `top` or `vmstat`.

Dynamic tracing tools like `systemtap` and `eBPF` (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) offer unparalleled visibility into the kernel and user-space without requiring kernel recompilation or application modification. These tools allow you to instrument specific kernel functions, system calls, or user-space functions, collecting data and even modifying behavior on the fly. `systemtap` uses a scripting language (`stap`) to define probes and actions. For example, a `systemtap` script could count how many times a specific kernel function is called, or log arguments passed to a system call. `eBPF` is a newer, more secure, and more efficient technology that allows user-space programs to run sandboxed code within the kernel. Tools built on `eBPF`, such as `bpftrace` or the `bcc` (BPF Compiler Collection) tools, provide powerful one-liners for common debugging scenarios, like `execsnoop` (to see new processes), `opensnoop` (to see file opens), or `biolatency` (to measure block I/O latency). These tools are incredibly powerful for diagnosing elusive performance issues, deadlocks, or unexpected system behavior. Safety note: Misusing `systemtap` or `eBPF` can potentially destabilize the kernel or lead to security vulnerabilities if not handled carefully. Always use them in a controlled environment first.

A structured approach is paramount when debugging complex issues. Start by gathering all available information: logs, `dmesg`, `systemctl status`, `top`, `ss`, etc. Formulate a hypothesis about the root cause. Then, use targeted tools (like `GDB`, `perf`, `strace`, `eBPF` tools) to test that hypothesis. Isolate the problem by simplifying the environment or reproducing it in a controlled setting. For multi-component systems (e.g., a web application with a database and caching layer), use a "divide and conquer" strategy: verify each component works in isolation before investigating their interactions. Document findings, even dead ends, as they can inform future troubleshooting efforts. The ability to combine these advanced tools with a systematic, logical approach is the hallmark of an expert Linux troubleshooter.

screens.title: Advanced Debugging Techniques & Tools
screens.subtitle: From core dumps to eBPF: diagnosing crashes and performance anomalies

narration.text: In this chapter we move beyond simple log checks and into tools that inspect program and kernel behavior directly. You’ll learn how to use the GNU Debugger to perform post-mortem analysis on core dumps and attach to running processes safely, how to use perf to record call graphs and identify C P U hotspots, and how systemtap and eBPF let you trace kernel and user-space events without rebuilding the kernel. These skills matter when bugs are intermittent or performance anomalies hide across multiple components. For example, a segmentation fault captured in a core dump reveals the exact stack and variable values at crash time, while a perf profile can show that a busy loop is monopolizing C P U cycles even when top looks innocuous. Throughout, I’ll emphasize a structured approach: gather evidence, form a hypothesis, test with targeted tools, and isolate components. That way you avoid noisy guessing and can reproduce and fix issues with confidence. As you follow the demos, think about which tool gives the specific evidence you need: a call stack, a counter, or a live trace.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Combine post-mortem inspection, performance profiling, and dynamic tracing with a disciplined hypothesis-driven workflow to resolve complex Linux issues.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to inspect crashed programs with GDB, including loading core dumps and extracting full backtraces and variable values. You’ll also be able to attach to live processes for diagnosis with the necessary caution in production. You will learn to collect and interpret perf recordings to discover C P U hot spots and call graphs that reveal where cycles are spent. Finally, you will be introduced to dynamic tracing via systemtap and eBPF so you can probe kernel and user-space behavior without rebuilding the kernel. Each objective pairs tool skills with a decision: when to use post-mortem inspection, when to profile with perf, and when to trace events with eBPF. These choices are crucial: the right tool gives precise evidence, the wrong one wastes time or risks stability. Expect short exercises and a scenario where you reproduce a segfault, analyze a core dump, and then profile the same program to find a busy loop.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Practice
screens.subtitle: How you'll apply the tools in real scenarios

narration.text: These objectives translate tool knowledge into a repeatable debug workflow. First, gather evidence: logs, dmesg, systemctl status, and any core files. Second, form a hypothesis about the cause — is it memory corruption, an input and output stall, or a logic bug? Third, select the right tool: GDB for state at crash, perf for C P U distribution, and eBPF tools for tracing system calls or file opens. Fourth, isolate components in multi-service environments using divide-and-conquer so you don’t chase symptoms across services. You will practice by compiling a test C program with debug symbols, forcing a segfault to produce a core dump, and then inspecting that core. You’ll also profile the same program to contrast a correctness bug with a performance issue. A careful habit: document assumptions and dead ends. Those notes save time later and make your debugging reproducible. Think of debugging as experimentation with instrumentation and repeatable steps.

keyIdea.title: Applied focus
keyIdea.text: Turn tool commands into hypothesis-driven experiments and document findings for reproducibility.

screens.title: What is deep debugging?
screens.subtitle: From logs to program state and kernel events

narration.text: Deep debugging means moving from surface evidence, such as logs and process lists, into the concrete internal state of a program or the kernel. At its core is the idea of state inspection: what values were on the stack, which threads were active, and which kernel events occurred just before failure. A concrete example is a segmentation fault: a log entry might say the process crashed, but a core dump and GDB reveal the exact function call sequence and the pointer value that was dereferenced. A common misconception is that more logging always solves hard bugs. In reality logging adds overhead and may change timing; it also might miss the exact moment when transient memory corruption occurs. Deep debugging uses tools that capture the program’s state, or its behavior at the kernel level, without relying solely on prior logging. Why this matters: with access to a backtrace and variable values you can map a crash to a specific source line and reason about fixes rather than guessing. Takeaway: prefer targeted, stateful evidence—core dumps, profilers, or probes—over indiscriminate logging when diagnosing intermittent or complex failures.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Deep debugging exposes internal program or kernel state so you can identify root causes, not just symptoms.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is deep debugging?
From logs to program state and kernel events
Definition
State inspection
Stack traces, local variables, thread states, and registers provide definitive evidence about a crash.
Kernel visibility
Trace system calls, scheduling, and I/O events with systemtap or eBPF for system-wide anomalies.
Avoid over-logging
Excessive logging can change timing and mask intermittent bugs.
Concrete example
A process crashes with a segfault. Reading system logs only shows the crash time. Loading the core dump in GDB reveals the exact function and the null pointer that was dereferenced, turning an opaque symptom into a fixable code change.
Key Takeaway

Stateful evidence is stronger than logs for intermittent or low-observable faults.

screens.title: GDB for post-mortem analysis
screens.subtitle: Loading core dumps, backtraces, and inspecting variables

narration.text: GDB is the standard tool for post-mortem debugging: it lets you load an executable and its core dump to examine the program state when it crashed. Start by ensuring the executable has debug symbols. Without them GDB will show addresses instead of source lines and variable names. A simple workflow: compile with debug symbols, enable core dumps, run the program to crash, then run gdb with the executable and core file. In GDB, the backtrace command shows the call stack; backtrace full displays local variables for each frame. For example, if crash_function dereferenced a null pointer, bt full reveals the frame and the value of that pointer. A common misconception is that core dumps are useless for optimized builds — while optimizations can inline or rearrange code, debug symbols still provide much more insight than no symbols. Also remember to match the exact executable and source version to the core file. When working on production-like systems, capture core dumps to a controlled directory and avoid leaving sensitive full memory files exposed. Follow-up steps include setting breakpoints, examining memory with x/g and printing variables with print, and iterating until your hypothesis explains the observed state. How would you confirm that the variable value caused the crash rather than a different frame? Use the backtrace and variable inspection together to test that claim.

keyIdea.title: GDB takeaway
keyIdea.text: Core dumps plus debug symbols give precise evidence of where and why a program crashed.

content.html:
Process Flow
GDB for post-mortem analysis
Load cores, inspect backtraces, inspect variables
Hands-on commands
Workflow steps
  • Compile with debug symbols: add -g so GDB can map addresses to source.
  • Enable core dumps and set a safe core_pattern and ulimit -c unlimited.
  • Run the program to produce core, then load it: gdb <executable> <core-file>.
  • Use bt full to see the stack and local variables, then inspect frames and memory.
  • Document the backtrace and reproduce in a controlled build if possible.
Common mistake
Not installing or using debug-symbol builds makes GDB output much less useful.
Example commands
# Compile with debug symbols
gcc -g -o my_app my_app.c

# Enable core dumps and pattern
sudo sysctl -w kernel.core_pattern="/tmp/core-%e-%p-%t"
ulimit -c unlimited

# Run to crash and then analyze
./my_app
gdb my_app /tmp/core-my_app-12345
Key Takeaway

Always use debug-symbol builds and keep core files accessible to enable precise source-level diagnosis.

screens.title: Safe live debugging and common pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Attaching to running processes and production caution

narration.text: Attaching a debugger to a running process gives powerful live insight but carries risks. The attach operation can pause the target process or threads, change timing, and in production create customer-visible pauses. Use attach only when you can tolerate a pause or when working in a controlled environment. For production troubleshooting prefer read-only profilers or low-overhead tracing when possible. A concrete example: using gdb attach PID to inspect a hung worker will stop threads and may trigger timeouts in other services. If you must attach, notify stakeholders, and prefer non-intrusive reads such as /proc/pid/maps and /proc/pid/status first. A frequent misconception is that debugging a single thread is harmless; in multi-threaded servers, pausing one thread can cause deadlocks or request timeouts. Another safe practice is to run debuggers on a copy of memory when supported, or use core dump capture for later analysis. Finally, always ensure debug symbols and source alignment with the running binary; otherwise live inspection is less informative. Closing question: when would you prefer a perf recording or an eBPF probe over attaching GDB? The answer lies in the trade-off between required state detail and acceptable impact on the running service.

keyIdea.title: Safety note
keyIdea.text: Attaching stops execution and can change behavior — prefer low-impact tools on production systems when possible.

content.html:
Definition
Safe live debugging and common pitfalls
When to attach, when to avoid it
Production caution
When to attach
  • Controlled test environment or maintenance window.
  • When you need exact runtime values and stack for a live state bug.
  • Short, well-coordinated inspection with stakeholders informed.
Alternatives
Use perf recordings, strace for syscalls, or eBPF probes when you need low-impact visibility.
Pitfalls & checklist
- Attaching pauses threads and can cause timeouts.
- Missing debug symbols reduces value of inspection.
- Live memory modifications can alter behavior; avoid unless needed.
- Capture a core if you need to minimize runtime disturbance and analyze offline.
Pro Tip

If possible, replicate the issue in a staging environment and attach there to avoid production impact.

screens.title: perf for profiling and call graphs
screens.subtitle: Collecting perf record -g and analyzing with perf report

narration.text: perf is the kernel-supplied profiling toolset that samples C P U and kernel events, producing data you can analyze to find hot functions and call graphs. Use perf stat for quick counters about a command’s execution, particularly cache misses and cycles. For deeper analysis, perf record -g runs the command and records call graph samples; perf report then visualizes the hottest functions and the call hierarchy. A practical example: run perf record -g./my_app while the program executes its busy loop; even if the program later crashes, perf. data will include samples up to the crash. A common misconception is that perf only reports user-space functions; with proper privileges and options, perf can attribute kernel time and show kernel call paths. Also remember to run perf with sudo when recording system-wide events or hardware counters. Interpreting results: look for functions with high C P U percentage and wide inclusive time in the call graph; these are hotspots useful for optimization. When many small functions consume time, inline expansion or algorithmic fixes may be necessary. Finally, perf top offers interactive real-time sampling when you need immediate feedback on hot symbols. Takeaway: perf finds where cycles are spent so you can focus optimization effort on genuine hotspots rather than premature micro-optimization.

keyIdea.title: perf takeaway
keyIdea.text: Use perf record -g and perf report to reveal the call graph and identify true CPU hotspots for optimization.

content.html:
Process Flow
perf for profiling and call graphs
Record call graphs, view hotspots, and profile across kernel and user space.
perf record → perf report
Quick reference
  • perf stat <command> — summary counters for a run.
  • sudo perf record -g <command> — record samples plus call graphs.
  • perf report — analyze perf.data and inspect call stacks and percentages.
  • perf top — live, top-like view of hottest symbols.
Misconception
Believing perf replaces functional debugging. perf shows where time is spent, not why logic is incorrect.
Example terminal steps
# Record a program with call graphs
sudo perf record -g ./my_app

# After run completes
perf report

# System-wide recording for 30s
sudo perf record -a -g sleep 30
perf report
Key Takeaway

Use call-graph sampling to prioritize optimization on functions that consume the most CPU, not guesses.

screens.title: Prepare and reproduce: compile with -g and capture a core
screens.subtitle: A hands-on starter: my_app segfault and perf profile

narration.text: This hands-on activity prepares an experiment you will run and analyze. Start by creating a small C program that intentionally crashes and also has a C P U-intensive loop so you can practice both crash analysis and profiling. Compile with the -g flag to include debug symbols. Configure the system to produce core dumps by setting kernel. core_pattern and enabling unlimited core sizes with ulimit -c unlimited. Run the program to produce a core; then load it into gdb and run bt full to see the backtrace and local variables. Next, record a perf session with call graphs: perf record -g./my_app. Even if the program crashes, perf. data will contain samples up to the crash and you can run perf report to inspect which functions dominated C P U time. A useful contrast to note: gdb gives the exact program state at a crash, while perf gives statistical samples that point to hotspots; one is deterministic for the crash moment, the other is probabilistic over runtime. A common error is forgetting to compile with -g or to match the exact binary used to create the core; without that, symbols are missing. After you finish, clean up binaries and core files. Reflect: when did the crash occur relative to the busy loop, and what does that tell you about the bug versus performance design?

keyIdea.title: Practical prep
keyIdea.text: Compile with -g, enable cores, and record perf to get both deterministic crash state and probabilistic performance data.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Prepare and reproduce: compile with -g and capture a core
Segfault reproduction and perf profiling starter
Starter source (my_app.c)
// my_app.c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

void crash_function() {
  char *ptr = NULL;
  strcpy(ptr, "This will crash!");
}

void busy_loop() {
  long i;
  for (i = 0; i < 1000000000; i++) {
    ; // CPU intensive loop
  }
}

int main() {
  printf("Starting application...
");
  busy_loop();
  crash_function();
  return 0;
}
Commands to run
# Compile with debug symbols
gcc -g -o my_app my_app.c

# Prepare the system for core dumps (temporary)
sudo sysctl -w kernel.core_pattern="/tmp/core-%e-%p-%t"
ulimit -c unlimited

# Run to produce core
./my_app

# Analyze core
gdb my_app /tmp/core-my_app--
# (inside gdb) bt full

# Profile with perf
sudo perf record -g ./my_app
perf report
Key Takeaway

A controlled reproduce-and-record workflow gives both exact crash state and performance trends for effective debugging.

screens.title: systemtap: targeted probes without recompiling
screens.subtitle: A scripting approach to instrument kernel functions and user-space events

narration.text: systemtap provides a script-driven way to insert probes into a running kernel or user-space programs. Think of a probe as a lightweight hook that records arguments, counts calls, or logs events when a matched function or system call runs. A typical workflow is to write a small script in the stap language that declares probes and actions, then run it on a test system to gather counts or traces. For example, you might count invocations of a kernel function related to block input and output to understand latency spikes. A concrete example: a small script that counts how often a specific kernel function runs over 60 seconds can reveal unexpected loops in device drivers. Important practical notes: systemtap needs matching kernel debug info for the kernel you trace, and scripts run with elevated privileges, so test in a controlled environment first. A common misconception is that systemtap is always safe in production; in reality poorly written scripts can block or crash the system by doing expensive operations inside probes. Use lightweight actions—increment counters and buffer output rather than heavy string formatting inside hot probes. To summarize, systemtap is excellent when you want direct scripted probes and access to kernel internals; its power comes with responsibility and the need to validate scripts on non-production hosts. Reflect: when would you prefer a short systemtap probe over a perf-based sampling profile?

keyIdea.title: Why systemtap matters
keyIdea.text: Scripted, precise probes let you count and log kernel or user-space events without rebuilding code, but always validate scripts in a safe environment.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.10 › systemtap Basics
Core Idea
Scripted probes that inspect kernel and user events

Write stap scripts to declare probes and actions, then run them to collect counts or arguments. Requires privilege and matching kernel stabs for best results.

When to use
  • Count or log specific kernel function calls for intermittent faults.
  • Inspect syscall arguments or user-space function entry/exit with probes.
  • Collect contextual data where sampling misses rare events.
Common mistake

Doing expensive work inside a probe. Probes fire in hot paths; heavy actions can slow or destabilize the system.

Key Takeaway

Use systemtap for targeted, scriptable kernel/user probes; keep actions minimal and test off-production first.

Example stap script
Counts a kernel function over a short run
Demo
# stap example_count.stp
probe kernel.function("do_some_io") {
  ++count[probefunc()]
}

probe timer.ms(60000) {
  foreach (f in count) {
    printf("%s %d
", f, count[f])
  }
  exit()
}
Run
sudo stap example_count.stp
Output
Function name followed by invocation count for the interval.

screens.title: eBPF: safe, efficient in-kernel probes with bpftrace
screens.subtitle: Modern tracing that runs sandboxed code in the kernel for low overhead observability

narration.text: eBPF is a modern in-kernel virtual machine that lets you run small, verified programs inside the kernel in a safe way. Tools like bpftrace and the BCC collection provide higher-level front ends so you can write concise one-liners to trace syscalls, process events, or network activity. The key benefit is efficiency: eBPF programs are JIT-compiled and sandboxed, minimizing overhead compared to heavy probes. A concrete example is a bpftrace one-liner that prints every open syscall with the process name and filename; this can reveal which process is unexpectedly opening many files. An important practical distinction: bpftrace is sampling and event-driven — it excels at live observability and low-overhead tracing. A common misconception is that eBPF needs kernel recompilation; it does not. However, not all kernels expose the same helpers or tracepoints, so portability varies. Safety note: while eBPF is designed to be safe, running untrusted or complex trace programs without understanding them can still impact performance. When you need low-overhead, production-safe visibility, prefer eBPF; when you need scripted, flexible probes with full kernel symbol access, systemtap might be the right tool. Try a short bpftrace example on a development host and ask: what would you choose when tracking a rare, short-lived syscall versus a long-running C P U hotspot?

keyIdea.title: Why eBPF matters
keyIdea.text: eBPF provides efficient, sandboxed in-kernel tracing; bpftrace makes it approachable with concise one-liners for live observability.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.10 › eBPF & bpftrace
Quick tour
bpftrace one-liners

bpftrace offers terse expressions to attach to tracepoints, kprobes, or uprobes and print arguments or timestamps. They are ideal for short, live diagnostics.

# Print process and filename for every open syscall
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat { printf("%s %s
", comm, str(args->filename)); }'

# Show top functions by count for 10 seconds
sudo bpftrace -e 'kprobe:do_sys_open { @[comm]++ } interval:s:10 { exit() }'
Run
Use sudo; prefer dev or staging for experiments.
Output
Live lines printed for each matched event; aggregated maps for counts.
Comparing choices
When to choose bpftrace
Low-overhead, live tracing for I/O, syscalls, and sched events; concise diagnostics in production-safe mode.
Safety note
Avoid heavy loops in probes; prefer maps and post-processing. Validate on non-production kernels first.
Pro tip
Use bpftrace aggregated maps for counts and export results rather than printing million lines in high-frequency paths.

screens.title: Choosing the right tool: strace, gdb, perf, or eBPF
screens.subtitle: Match the problem to the tool: behavior, performance, or crash analysis

narration.text: Choosing the right tool is a practical skill: each tool addresses a different class of problem. Start with a clear hypothesis about what you need to observe. If you need to see every system call and its arguments for a single process, strace gives precise syscall-level traces and is straightforward for debugging incorrect file access or permission failures. For crashes and source-level investigation of a C program, GDB lets you inspect the exact stack, variables, and memory in a core dump or attached live process. For performance hotspots where C P U usage is distributed across many small functions or across the kernel, perf's sampling and call-graph recording helps you find functions consuming the most C P U cycles. For low-overhead, scalable tracing across kernel and user-space with safe in-kernel execution, eBPF tools like bpftrace are ideal. A concrete scenario: a daemon crashes with a segfault—use GDB and core dumps to find the faulty line. If instead the server is slow but no single process shows obvious C P U, run sudo perf record -a -g sleep 30 and then perf report to inspect call graphs. A frequent misconception is to reach for GDB for everything; GDB is powerful but heavyweight and may not show system-wide scheduling or kernel-level patterns. In practice combine tools: use strace to confirm syscall failures, perf to find hotspots, and eBPF to trace kernel interactions. Close with this question: which first-step tool would you pick for a high-frequency short syscall you cannot reproduce locally?

keyIdea.title: Tool pairing insight
keyIdea.text: Hypothesis first: use lightweight tracing to confirm, sampling for hotspots, and GDB for line-level crash analysis.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.10 › Tool Selection
Quick comparison
strace
Trace syscalls and arguments for a single process; good for file/permission failures and short reproductions.
gdb
Source-level debugging and core dump inspection; use for crashes and memory errors when you have debug symbols.
perf
Sampling profiler for CPU hotspots and call graphs across user-space and kernel; use perf record & perf report.
eBPF / bpftrace
Low-overhead, in-kernel tracing for high-frequency events, syscalls, and aggregated metrics in production.
Scenario mapping
Intermittent segfault in C daemon
Generate core, load in gdb with debug symbols and run bt full to inspect the exact line and variable state.
System-wide CPU but no single top process
Use sudo perf record -a -g sleep 30 then perf report to find code paths consuming cycles across processes.
High-rate open syscalls from unknown process
Run bpftrace one-liner to print process and filename for open calls and identify the offender with low overhead.

screens.title: A methodical workflow for complex, multi-component issues
screens.subtitle: Hypothesis → isolate → instrument → test → confirm → document

narration.text: Debugging complex systems is less about a single command and more about a reproducible, logical workflow. Begin by gathering all available evidence: logs, dmesg, systemctl outputs, and recent deployments. Formulate a concise hypothesis: a statement that explains the failure in a way you can test. For example, hypothesize that the web application is blocked on database connections after a specific commit. Next, isolate components: run the web app with a local database, or run the database and client independently to confirm each behaves as expected. Then pick targeted instrumentation to test the hypothesis—strace to inspect syscalls, perf to find C P U hotspots, or eBPF to count network or file events. Run focused tests that reproduce the fault in a controlled environment and collect trace artifacts. Analyze results: did the traces support or refute your hypothesis? If refuted, refine the hypothesis and iterate. Finally, document both findings and dead ends; a precise record shortens future troubleshooting. A common mistake is running many heavy probes at once; it creates noise and may change system behavior. Instead, narrow the scope and add instrumentation incrementally. As a reflective question: after your first iteration, what minimal evidence would convince you the hypothesis is correct or wrong?

keyIdea.title: Workflow benefit
keyIdea.text: A repeatable, hypothesis-driven approach reduces wasted effort and makes intermittent faults tractable across interacting services.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.10 › Structured Debugging
Step-by-step
1. Gather evidence
Collect logs, dmesg, system status, and any core dumps before changing the system.
2. Formulate hypothesis
Write a testable statement about the root cause, e.g., a deadlock in the cache layer after a config change.
3. Isolate components
Run components in isolation or with mocks to confirm which element reproduces the fault.
4. Instrument & test
Apply targeted tracing: strace for syscalls, perf for CPU hotspots, or eBPF for kernel events.
5. Analyze & iterate
Interpret traces against your hypothesis. Refine and repeat until the cause is identified.
Check your understanding
You have an intermittent latency spike affecting only the API service. Which minimal test would you run first and why?

screens.title: Live terminal demo: GDB, perf, and a bpftrace one-liner
screens.subtitle: Follow a paired walkthrough: post-mortem + profiling + live tracing

narration.text: This walkthrough ties the prior concepts together with concrete terminal commands you can run in a development environment. Start with a program compiled with debug symbols and configured to allow core dumps. After the program crashes and produces a core file, run gdb with the executable and core file to get a full backtrace: the command is gdb my_app /tmp/core-... and then bt full inside gdb. The backtrace identifies the call stack and variable values at the crash point, which helps pinpoint the faulty line. For profiling, use perf record -g./my_app or sudo perf record -a -g sleep 10 for system-wide recording; then run perf report to inspect the call graph and find hot functions like busy_loop. perf top is useful for an interactive, real-time view. Finally, demonstrate a bpftrace one-liner to capture high-rate events with low overhead. For example, a simple bpftrace expression can print every open syscall with process name and filename; run it on a staging host and observe which process is opening many files. After collecting artifacts, compress or move trace files to a analysis host and document steps taken. A common pitfall is forgetting debug symbols or running gdb without the matching source; always keep the exact build and sources when debugging. End by asking: which artifact would you preserve after a crash to shorten future investigations?

keyIdea.title: Demo essential
keyIdea.text: Combine core backtrace, perf call graphs, and low-overhead eBPF traces to triangulate faults across code and system behavior.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.10 › Terminal Demo
Post-mortem with GDB
# Load core and get full backtrace
gdb my_app /tmp/core-my_app--
# (gdb) bt full

# Inspect a local variable and source context
# (gdb) frame 2
# (gdb) list
# (gdb) print some_variable
Keep the exact binary with -g and the source that was compiled. Without symbols, gdb shows addresses only.
Profile with perf
# Record a command with call graphs
perf record -g ./my_app
perf report

# System-wide 30s sampling
sudo perf record -a -g sleep 30
sudo perf report
Use -g for call graphs. Root may be required for system-wide kernel counters.
Live tracing: bpftrace one-liner
# Print process and filename for open syscalls
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat { printf("%s %s
", comm, str(args->filename)); }'

# Aggregated count example
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat { @[comm]++ } interval:s:5 { print(@); clear(@) }'
Always test bpftrace scripts on non-production hosts when possible.
Save perf.data, core dumps, and bpftrace outputs as artifacts for future analysis.

screens.subtitle: Concise definitions to keep in your troubleshooting toolbox

narration.text: Keep a short mental map of the core tools and ideas. GDB is your source-level inspector and post-mortem tool when you have debug symbols and a core dump. A core dump captures the process memory and stack at crash time and is invaluable for reproducing a fault offline. perf is the go-to sampling profiler for C P U and kernel events; it reveals hotspots and call-graph structure. systemtap provides scripted probes for detailed kernel and user-space event collection when you need explicit instrumentation. Each of these tools serves a different role: use the one that best tests your hypothesis. Storing symbols, preserving artifacts, and documenting dead ends are practices as important as running the commands. Which artifact would you archive first after a crash? That discipline shortens future investigations. Key Concepts means match hypothesis to the right tool and always preserve symbols, core files, and trace artifacts.. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. Keep a short, prioritized set of artifacts: core files, perf.data, and concise trace outputs. They speed root-cause analysis and make your debugging reproducible.

narration.text: Remember these practical safety and workflow rules. systemtap gives flexible scripted probes but requires careful testing because scripts can affect kernel behavior. eBPF and bpftrace offer lower overhead, but ensure your kernel supports required helpers and always test scripts without enabling heavy output on production. A structured debugging method—evidence, hypothesis, isolate, instrument, test, document—keeps teams aligned and prevents wasted work. Finally, preserve debug symbols and artifacts: a binary without symbols severely reduces the value of a core dump. These practices separate expert troubleshooters from those who guess and hope. Ask yourself: what single artifact would you collect first to shorten the next investigation?
